novice.title: Novice Engineer
novice.blurb: A five minute orientation: what the four categories are and how the ladder works.
novice.body:
Welcome

This tree covers the fundamentals of software engineering: the skills that stay useful no matter which language, framework, or company you end up in. This page takes about five minutes and explains what you are looking at and how to use it.

The four categories

The tree you came from has four columns. Each one is a category: a single discipline, taught in four steps.

  • Code Craft: writing code that other people can read and change.
  • Design: deciding how the pieces of a program fit together.
  • Testing: proving that your code does what you think it does.
  • Delivery: getting your work off your machine and in front of real people.

These four are a loop, not a list. You write something, you shape it, you prove it works, you ship it, and what you learn from shipping changes how you write the next thing. That is why they sit side by side instead of one after another.

How the ladder works

Every category climbs the same four rungs, and a rung means the same thing in every column:

  • Basic (about 30 minutes): you know what the thing is and why it matters.
  • Foundational (1-2 hours): you can do it with some guidance.
  • Skilled (2-3 hours): you can do it on your own and make sound calls.
  • Advanced (4+ hours): you can handle the hard cases and teach it.

Nothing here is locked. You can open and read any module at any time, in any order. The only thing that is ordered is completion: a box turns green when you pass its quiz, and each quiz opens once the tier below it is green.

Where to start

Finish this page, take the short check below, and then pick whichever Basic module looks most interesting. The four Basic modules do not depend on each other, so start with the one you are most curious about. Curiosity beats discipline for getting through material like this.

What Master means

When you have finished the Advanced tier of all four categories, the Master module opens. It is not more reading. It is a final exam that pulls the four disciplines together, because in real work they never show up one at a time.

modules.title: Coupling and Cohesion
modules.blurb: The two words behind almost every design conversation, with no jargon required.
modules.body:
What "design" means in software

Software design has nothing to do with how things look. It is about how a program is arranged: what the pieces are, what each piece is responsible for, and how they connect. Every program has a design, whether anyone chose it or not. The only question is whether it was arranged on purpose or by accident.

Why care? Because programs change. New features, fixed bugs, new requirements nobody predicted. A program's design is really a prediction about how expensive those future changes will be. Good design makes the next change cheap. Bad design makes every change a small demolition project.

Coupling: how much the pieces know about each other

Think about a television and its remote. The remote knows almost nothing about the TV: it sends a handful of signals, and any TV that understands those signals will work. You can replace either one without touching the other. That is low coupling: two things connected through a small, well-defined channel.

Now imagine the remote was wired into the TV's circuit board, soldered to specific components. Replacing either one means opening up both. That is high coupling: two things that know so much about each other's insides that they can only change together.

Code works exactly the same way. When one part of a program reaches into the internal details of another, a change to either forces a change to both. You feel high coupling as: "I only wanted to change one small thing, and now half the codebase is complaining."

Cohesion: whether things belong together

Open a well-organised kitchen drawer: forks with forks, knives with knives. You can find anything instantly, and putting things away is obvious. Now open the junk drawer: batteries, takeaway menus, a screwdriver, mystery keys. Nothing in it relates to anything else, and nobody can say what the drawer is for.

Cohesion is the measure of which drawer your code is. A cohesive module contains things that genuinely belong together and can be described in one sentence: "this handles payments." A low-cohesion module is a junk drawer, and its name usually gives it away: utils, helpers, misc.

The two ideas point in opposite directions on purpose. You want the pieces of a program loosely connected to each other (low coupling) and tightly related inside themselves (high cohesion). Almost every design conversation you will ever have is these two words wearing different costumes.

The one question to carry with you

Long before you can name the patterns, you can ask the beginner's most powerful design question: "If I change this, what else breaks?" If the answer is "nothing" or "one obvious thing nearby", the design is doing its job. If the answer is "who knows", you have found high coupling, and you now understand what everyone in the code review is arguing about.

Do not over-apply this yet. Beginners who learn about coupling sometimes start splitting everything into tiny disconnected pieces, which creates its own mess. At this stage, just learn to see it. The instinct for when to act on it comes at the next tiers.

modules.title: Naming and Readable Structure
modules.blurb: Why code is written for readers, and the three habits that make it readable.
modules.body:
Code is read far more than it is written

Here is the most useful thing to know before writing your first serious line of code: you will write it once, and it will be read many times. By teammates, by reviewers, by whoever maintains it after you move on, and most often by a future version of you who remembers nothing about it. Every choice that makes code easier to read is paid back every single time someone reads it.

This is why experienced engineers obsess over things that look cosmetic to beginners: names, layout, and size. They are not being fussy. They are optimising for the reader, because the reader is who the code is really for. The computer would be equally happy with one long line of gibberish.

Names carry the meaning

A name is the one piece of documentation that cannot drift out of date without someone noticing, because it sits right there in the code. Compare these two lines, which do exactly the same thing:

const d = t - l;
const daysSinceLastLogin = today - lastLoginDate;

The first line forces every reader to go hunting for what d, t, and l mean. The second one answers the question before it is asked. Nothing about the program changed. Everything about the reading experience did.

A good name says what something is or what it is for, not how it came to be. A list called filteredResults2 tells you its history. A list called activeCustomers tells you its meaning.

Rename freely. If you read a name and it surprises you, or you have to look at the code to understand it, rename it on the spot. Modern editors rename everything in one action, so the cost is near zero and the payoff lasts forever.

Shape: small pieces with one job

Long blocks of code are hard to read for the same reason long sentences without punctuation are hard to read: you have to hold everything in your head at once. The fix is the same in both cases. Break it up.

A function should do one thing, and its name should say what that thing is. When a function does one thing, you can read the name instead of the body, and suddenly a screen of code reads like a short list of steps rather than a puzzle. When you find yourself describing a function with the word "and", that is usually two functions living in one.

Comments explain why, not what

Beginners often comment every line, describing what the code does. But the code already says what it does, and readers can see it. What the code cannot say is why: why this approach and not the obvious one, why this strange-looking special case, why this order matters. Those are the comments worth writing, because they capture the thinking that would otherwise be lost.

A wrong comment is worse than no comment. Code that changes while its comment stays behind produces a comment that lies, and readers tend to believe comments. If you write one, treat it as part of the code and keep it true.

Consistency beats cleverness

Teams agree on formatting and naming conventions not because one style is objectively best but because sameness is readable. When every file looks the same, differences jump out, and differences are where the information is. This is also why most teams use automatic formatters: they end every argument about style by making the machine decide.

That is the whole Basic idea of code craft: write for the person reading, name things for what they mean, keep pieces small, explain the why, and be boringly consistent. Everything deeper in this category builds on those habits.

modules.title: What a Test Actually Proves
modules.blurb: What a test is, why clicking around does not scale, and the one question that matters.
modules.body:
A test is a program that checks a program

Strip away the tooling and jargon and a software test is a very simple thing: a small program whose only job is to run part of your program and check that it did the right thing. "Call the discount function with a total of 100 and a 10 percent coupon. Did it return 90? Yes: pass. No: fail." That is the entire idea.

Once tests are written down as code, a computer can run thousands of them in seconds, every time anything changes. That speed is the whole point, as you are about to see.

Why not just try it by hand?

You can, and everyone does at first. Run the app, click around, see if it works. The problem is not that manual checking is wrong. The problem is that it does not scale, in three specific ways:

  • You forget. Nobody remembers all forty things they checked last month, so nobody rechecks them all.
  • It is slow. Ten minutes of clicking, repeated after every change, quietly becomes the most expensive part of the work.
  • Changes break old things. The bug you introduce today is usually in something that worked yesterday, which is exactly the thing you no longer bother to check.

Written tests fix all three at once. They never forget, they run in seconds, and they recheck everything, every time. A good test suite is a safety net that lets you change code without fear, and fearless change is what keeps software alive.

What a passing test actually proves

Here is the part beginners are rarely told. A passing test proves one thing only: the specific facts this test checked were true on this run. It does not prove the program is correct, or bug-free, or safe. It proves the discount function returned 90 for that one input. Every claim beyond that is hope, not evidence.

Green does not mean correct. A test that checks the wrong thing, or checks nothing at all, passes just as brightly as a good one. A wall of passing tests is only as meaningful as the questions those tests ask.

The one question that separates good tests from decoration

For any test, ask: "If the code it covers broke, would this test fail?" If yes, the test is doing its job: it is an alarm wired to something real. If no, the test is decoration. It costs time to run and maintain and it protects nothing.

This question needs no experience to ask and it will carry you a long way. It is also the seed of everything in the higher tiers of this category, where the craft becomes choosing which questions are worth asking.

Name tests after the rule they prove. A test called expiredCouponsAreRejected documents a rule of the system. A test called test3 documents nothing, and will outlive everyone who knew what it meant.

modules.title: Version Control as Communication
modules.blurb: Save points, commits, and why a commit message is a letter to your future self.
modules.body:
What version control is

Version control is a system that keeps a complete history of a project: every change, who made it, when, and why. Think of it as save points in a game, except you can have thousands of them, jump back to any of them, and see exactly what changed between any two. The tool nearly everyone uses is called git, and the projects it tracks are called repositories.

Each save point is called a commit. A commit bundles up a set of changes with a short message describing them. String the commits together and you get the story of the project, told one change at a time.

Why bother, if it is just you?

Beginners often meet version control as a team tool and assume it matters only for teams. But even alone, it gives you three things nothing else does:

  • Undo that actually works. Broke everything at 11pm? Jump back to the commit where it worked. No more project-final-v2-REAL.zip.
  • Freedom to experiment. Try the risky idea. If it fails, throw it away cleanly instead of untangling it by hand.
  • A searchable memory. "When did this break?" and "why is this line here?" become questions with answers.

A commit is a message to a person

Here is the mental shift that separates people who use git from people who use it well: a commit is not a save button. It is a message to a future reader. That reader is often you, months from now, staring at a bug and asking "what was I thinking here?" The commit message is where the answer lives, if you wrote one.

The convention is simple. The first line says what changed, briefly: "Reject expired coupons at checkout." The lines after it, when needed, say why: what was broken, what constraint drove the approach, what you tried that did not work. The code shows what changed anyway. The why exists nowhere else.

Messages like "fix", "stuff", and "asdf" are all the same message: "I did not expect anyone to read this." Someone will read it, probably during a bad week, and that someone is most likely you.

Small commits tell better stories

One commit should contain one logical change. Fixed a bug and also renamed some files and also tweaked a colour? That is three commits. Small commits can be understood at a glance, undone individually, and searched precisely. A commit that does five things can only be taken or rejected as a lump.

A good habit from day one: before you commit, read the first line out loud. If it needs the word "and", split the commit. The discipline takes seconds and it makes the history readable forever.

Where this goes

Everything in the Delivery category builds on this foundation. Sharing work with a team, reviewing each other's changes, shipping to real users automatically: all of it rides on a clean, honest history. Learn to leave good save points now and every later tier gets easier.
